cycles.name: Hard Stop
focuses: Build eccentric braking control and single-leg quality. Learn to absorb force before we ask you to produce it.
Posterior chain and loaded pulling as real working volume. No horizontal pressing this cycle.
Film your top set on the back squat and the RDL every week, and log sleep quality and bodyweight.

paragraphs: You already spend 10 to 15 hours a week on court. Your body knows how to move fast. What it almost never gets is heavy, slow, controlled work, and that gap is what we're filling here.

This cycle is about stopping. Every ball you chase ends with you putting the brakes on, and the leg that absorbs that is the leg that keeps you on court. So the tempo is slow on purpose. Three seconds down on the big lifts. If you're used to just moving the weight up and down, this will feel strange for a week.
Your job in week one is simple. Find your weights, film your top sets, and don't chase numbers. We build the brakes first. Cycle two is where we spend it.
outcomes: Real working weights logged on all three main lifts
Three seconds of control on every squat and RDL rep
Cleared technique film on both barbell lifts
Sleep quality and bodyweight logged every week
Single-leg strength that holds when you push off wide
A base that's ready for real load in Force Bank

cycles.name: Force Bank
focuses: Maximal force in free-standing bilateral and split-stance patterns. The deepest strength window of the arc.
Low-dose rotational throws and jumps every week so you never go a block without a fast rep.

paragraphs: Cycle two is where we cash this in.

Once you can control the weight on the way down, we start loading it properly. This is the deepest strength block of your year, and it's the one that changes how much force your legs can put into the ground. That's your serve and your first step.
You might feel a bit slow before you feel fast. That's normal and it passes.
Earn it in these five weeks.

cycles.name: Whip Crack
focuses: Rate of force development and kinetic-chain sequencing. Moderate loads moved with maximal intent.
One heavy exposure a week so the force base doesn't drain. Lateral push-off and first-step work.

cycles.name: Third Set
focuses: Repeat-power quality. Short clusters at full intent with full recovery, so the ceiling still exists on the fortieth hard ball.
Reactive multi-directional work, plus one maintenance exposure each of force and rate of force development.

cycles.name: Anvil
focuses: Back to maximal force in the same patterns, now against materially higher numbers.
Hold the power built in cycles three and four with one throw session and one reactive exposure a week.

exercises.name: Barbell Back Squat

good: Push the floor apart with your feet as you stand up
Feel your whole trunk lock tight before you go down
bad: Don't let your heels lift, your knees fall in, or your lower back round at the bottom

exercises.note: Always ramp up first: empty bar for 8, then two lighter sets before your working weight. Set the rack safeties one inch below your lowest point, every single set, no exceptions. Go only as deep as your lower back stays flat, and that is your depth for now.

exercises.name: Single-Arm Dumbbell Row

good: Drive your elbow back toward your hip
Feel the squeeze between your shoulder blades

exercises.note: Hand and knee on the bench so your lower back is fully supported. You've already loaded it under the squat today, so this one has to stay strict.

good: Press straight out and hold. The band wants to twist you, don't let it
Feel your side abs fighting the pull
bad: Don't let your hips rotate or your ribs flare out

good: Walk tall, like a string is pulling the top of your head up
Feel the side away from the weight working to keep you straight

days.completionMessage: Your hamstrings are the reason you can stop hard and not tear something, and you just spent three seconds under load on every single rep. Expect them to talk to you tomorrow.

exercises.name: Barbell Romanian Deadlift

exercises.note: Double overhand grip, and use straps once your grip gives out before your hamstrings do. End the set the rep your back rounds, not when you run out of reps. That rounding rep is the only one that can hurt you.

exercises.name: Scapular Pull-Up

Feel your lats switch on at the bottom

exercises.note: Arms stay completely straight. This is only your shoulder blades pulling your body up an inch or two. It's the step that earns you a proper pull-up in cycle two, so don't rush past it.

exercises.note: Make it harder or easier by walking your feet forward or back. Don't change anything else.

cards.title: Film your top sets
cards.body:
I'm not standing next to you, so video is how I coach you. Every week, film your heaviest set of the back squat and the RDL and send it to me on WhatsApp. Phone on the floor, from the side, whole body in frame.

These two lifts are the ones that carry real load, and they're the two I've never seen you do. The weight on those two doesn't go up until I've watched the film and cleared it. That's not me being difficult. It's how I make sure you're 38 and still playing at 45.

If the videos stop coming, the weight stops moving. Everything else in the program you can just get on with.

cards.title: Week one is for finding your weights
cards.body:
The app never tells you what weight to lift, and that's on purpose. You find it against the effort target, and the RPE number on each card is what you're aiming for. RPE 8 means you finish the set knowing you had about two more reps in you. RPE 7 is about three.

On a movement that's new to you, start lighter than you think. Do the first set, see where it landed, then adjust. Being 10 kg light on set one costs you nothing. Being 10 kg heavy costs you the session.

After that, week to week it's simple:

  • Hit all the reps at or under the target effort, go up a small amount next week.
  • Effort was already at the ceiling, or you missed reps, stay at the same weight and do it again.
  • Bad sleep, heavy court week, body feels flat, drop the weight. That's you reading yourself correctly, not you failing.

In week one specifically, stay well short of the targets while I'm checking your film. Nothing is lost. We have 25 weeks.

cards.title: Two numbers every week
cards.body:
Two things I want from you weekly, and they take one minute. Both are numbers, not feelings, because feelings drift and numbers don't.

Sleep quality, out of 10. You told me 5, and that's the one soft spot in your whole file. Everything else about your recovery looks good. If that 5 turns into a 3 for a week, I'd rather change your program than have you grind through it.

Bodyweight, same day, same time, before breakfast. We are not trying to change it. 88 kg is your playing weight and I want it to stay there. I'm watching it because heavy leg work stacked on 15 hours of tennis burns a lot, and if the scale starts sliding down it usually means you're not eating enough for the work. That looks like getting lean and it's actually losing force.

cards.title: Tell me what talks to you
cards.body:
Your form says no injuries and no history, which is great. But before session one I want one honest answer from you.

What talks to you the morning after a hard court block? Heel, knee, elbow, low back, shoulder. Anything that you notice and then just play through. Most players who've been on court as long as you have something, and it's normal.

Telling me doesn't cost you anything. It never means I take training away from you. It means I pick a slightly different version of a movement so the thing doesn't get worse. That's it.

cards.title: When to change the plan
cards.body:
The program is written for a normal week. Here's what to do when the week isn't normal.

  • Feeling rough? Take one point off every RPE that day.
  • Short on time or really flat? Do the first jumping movement and the first main lift, then go home. But run the main lift at its easier version or just two sets. A bad day never carries a heavy barbell.
  • Two bad nights in a row before a heavy day? Same thing, short version only.
  • Playing the same day? Gym after tennis, or leave 4 to 6 hours between them.

You can move the days around your court schedule, with three rules that don't move:

  • Day 1 and Day 3 never land on back to back days. They both hammer the same part of your legs.
  • Leave at least 48 hours between any two gym sessions.
  • Day 2 is never the day before a match or a heavy court block. The RDL will make your hamstrings sore and you'll feel it when you push off.

cards.title: Week five you back off
cards.body:
Weeks one to four you build. Week five you cut the work roughly in half and keep the weight and the intent exactly the same.

So on the big lifts, do about half the sets you normally would, and do them properly. Don't make them lighter and don't slow down the intent. Easy weeks that drop the effort blunt the very thing we spent four weeks building.

This is also the week I read your logs and write cycle two. The better your logging, the better that program is.

cards.title: What this cycle will and won't do
cards.body:
Being straight with you, because there's no tournament date to point at and I'd rather you know the plan than guess at it.

Several things in this cycle are just being maintained, on purpose. Your conditioning, your rotation work, your fast footwork. You get all of that from 10 to 15 hours of tennis a week. If I put it in the gym as well I'd just be making you tired for no gain.

What you should get across the next few months is roughly 10 to 20 percent more strength in your legs and something like 8 to 15 cm on a standing broad jump. That's a real change in what you can put into the ground. Anyone promising you more than that is selling something.

What you'll notice first, probably around week three, is that you stop feeling wobbly when you have to stop hard and change direction. That's the whole point of this block.
